Front matter

A step-by-step guide to semiconductor spin-qubit experiments

From Chip to Qubit

How a spin-qubit experiment is really done, from a bonded chip to benchmarked two-qubit gates, and why each step comes where it does

A spin-qubit experiment is a long chain of measurements. Each one answers a single question about the device, and each answer is a number you need for the next step. This book walks that chain from beginning to end on one realistic device, so that by the end you know not only what labs do, but why they do it in that order and what each plot is telling you.

Version 1.0, October 2026. Written for a reader with undergraduate physics, mathematics and solid-state physics. Facts and typical numbers are taken from the research papers listed at the end; where a number depends strongly on the device, the text says so.

The story this book follows

Almost everything here is told through one device, which we simply call our device. It is the kind of device that most silicon spin-qubit groups use today: two quantum dots in an isotopically purified 28Si/SiGe heterostructure, defined by three layers of overlapping gates, with a cobalt micromagnet on top and a third, larger dot next to them that serves as a charge sensor. We take it from the moment the chip arrives in the lab to the moment two-qubit gates are benchmarked. Along the way you will meet the same gates, the same lever arms and the same frequencies again and again, so the numbers become familiar rather than abstract.

Two other devices appear when they teach something the silicon device cannot. A GaAs double dot shows how the field began, why nuclear spins matter, and how singlet–triplet qubits work in their original setting. A silicon triple dot shows how exchange-only qubits are operated. Holes in germanium get their own chapter, because they are now one of the most active platforms.

How to read it

Read Parts A to G in order the first time. They are one continuous experiment, and later chapters lean on numbers measured earlier. Part H can be read in any order once you have finished Part F. Part I is about keeping a working device working, which is where most lab time actually goes.

A few recurring elements help you keep your bearings:

Device passport

At the end of most chapters, a short table lists the numbers we have now measured on our device and where each will be used next. By Part G the passport is a complete description of a working two-qubit processor. Real labs keep exactly this kind of record.

Lab notebook

Short entries written the way an experimentalist writes them at the end of a session: what was measured, the settings, what looked odd. They show the rhythm of real work, including the false starts.

When it goes wrong

Each measurement can fail in a handful of typical ways. These boxes pair what you see with its usual cause and what to try. Appendix C collects all of them into one troubleshooting index.

Worked numbers

Calculations with real values, worked through step by step so you can repeat them with your own device's numbers.

Check yourself

Questions at the end of a chapter, with answers you can open. Try them before opening the answers; they are chosen to test the reasoning, not memory.

Sources and corrections

Facts that need a source carry a bracketed number like [1]. Click it to jump to the full reference in the References chapter at the end, where every entry has a link. The reviews by Hanson and co-workers [1], Zwanenburg and co-workers [2], Burkard, Ladd and co-workers [3], Stano and Loss [4], and Vigneau and co-workers on reflectometry [5] are the best companions to this book.

This book grew out of an earlier, shorter guide. Appendix D lists the errors in that guide that are corrected here, so that anyone who learned from it knows exactly what to unlearn.

Part A · The whole picture · Chapter 1

The whole experiment on one page

When a group says "we have a working spin qubit", it means they have a list of numbers: how well they can prepare the spin, how fast and how accurately they can rotate it, how long it remembers its state, and how reliably they can read it out. Every number on that list was measured, and every measurement needed numbers measured before it. This chapter lays out that chain once, from beginning to end, so the rest of the book never feels like a list of disconnected procedures.

1.1Start from the end

Imagine the last experiment in a long campaign: randomized benchmarking of a single spin qubit. You prepare the electron's spin pointing down, apply a random sequence of a few hundred rotations that should, ideally, bring it back to where it started, then measure it. You repeat this for many random sequences and many lengths, and the rate at which the result decays tells you the average error of one gate. The output is a single number, perhaps 99.85%.

Now ask what you needed in order to run that experiment. Three things, at least:

  1. You had to prepare a known spin state. That means you already knew how to load one electron into the dot with a known spin, either by letting it relax in a magnetic field or by an energy-selective trick that only lets one spin direction in.
  2. You had to rotate the spin by exactly the right angles. That means you knew the spin's resonance frequency to within a few kilohertz, the microwave amplitude that gives a 90° rotation, and the phase that defines the rotation axis.
  3. You had to measure the spin in one shot. That means you had a way to turn "up" or "down" into a charge signal, and a charge sensor fast and quiet enough to see a single electron move in microseconds.

Each of those, in turn, rests on something earlier. You cannot find the resonance frequency without a spin readout to tell you when you have hit it. You cannot read out a spin before you have a single electron trapped in a dot, with tunnelling rates to its neighbours set to the right values. You cannot trap a single electron without a charge sensor to count electrons. You cannot form a sensor without first making the device conduct at all. And none of it happens until the device is cold, wired and quiet. Followed backwards, the chain reaches all the way to the moment the chip is mounted on its circuit board.

Every measurement in a spin-qubit experiment exists to produce a number that a later measurement needs.

This is the single most useful idea for making sense of what an experimental group does all day. When you see someone spend a week measuring tunnelling rates, it is not because tunnelling rates are interesting in themselves (sometimes they are), but because the spin readout cannot be set up without them.

1.2The chain, forwards

Turned around, the chain becomes the order in which a new device is brought up. Figure 1.1 shows the stages, and the table after it lists the question each stage answers and the numbers it hands on.

StageThe question it answersTypical measurementNumbers carried forward
1 Ready and coldIs the device intact, wired, and at a low electron temperature?Room-temperature resistance checks, cooldown logs, line checksWhich gates and ohmics work; fridge base temperature
2 Signs of lifeDo the gates do what they were designed to do?Leakage sweeps, accumulation (turn-on) and pinch-off curves, Coulomb diamondsTurn-on and pinch-off voltages; lever arms; charging energy; electron temperature
3 A charge sensorCan we see one electron move, and how fast?Sensor Coulomb peak, then reflectometry resonance and signal-to-noiseSensor operating point; tank frequency; integration time for a given SNR
4 One electron eachDo we have exactly one electron in each qubit dot, and control over how they tunnel?Charge stability diagrams, virtual gates, interdot and dot–reservoir tunnel ratesVirtual gate matrix; (1,1) operating point; tunnel coupling; tunnel rates
5 Spin to chargeCan we tell spin up from spin down in a single shot?Elzerman or Pauli-blockade readout, readout histograms, T1Readout point, threshold, readout fidelity; T1; valley splitting
6 One qubitWhere is the resonance, and how coherent is the spin?EDSR spectroscopy, Rabi, Ramsey, Hahn echo, dynamical decouplingQubit frequencies; π and π/2 pulse parameters; T2*, T2; noise spectrum
7 Benchmarked gatesHow good are the single-qubit gates, really?AllXY, error amplification, randomized benchmarking, gate set tomographyCalibrated gate set; average gate fidelity; error budget
8 Two qubitsCan the spins be entangled with high fidelity?Exchange spectroscopy J(V), CZ or CNOT calibration, Bell states, 2-qubit benchmarkingJ versus barrier voltage; CZ pulse; phase corrections; 2-qubit fidelity

Notice the change halfway through. Stages 1 to 4 are all about charge: making electrons appear, counting them, choosing exactly how many sit in each dot and how easily they hop. The spin, which is the actual qubit, does not appear until stage 5. This surprises newcomers, but it is how every spin-qubit experiment works. A spin's magnetic moment is far too small to detect directly. All spin measurements are done by converting spin into charge, and that conversion only works once the charge configuration is under complete control. More than half the effort on a new device is spent before anyone measures a spin.

1.3Why the order is fixed

Some steps can be swapped or repeated, but most of the order is forced by dependencies. Figure 1.2 shows the main ones. Read it as "you need this to do that".

Three dependencies are worth spelling out, because they explain choices that otherwise look arbitrary:

  • The lever arm turns voltages into energies. Gate voltages are what you set, but physics happens in energy. A lever arm α of 0.1 eV/V means 1 mV on the plunger moves the dot level by 100 µeV. Without it you cannot know whether a 0.5 mV step moves the level by more or less than the Zeeman energy, and spin readout depends on exactly that comparison. So the lever arm is measured early (Chapter 8), and almost every later chapter uses it.
  • Electron temperature limits readout. Spin readout distinguishes two energies separated by the Zeeman energy. If the electrons in the reservoir are thermally smeared over a comparable energy, the wrong spin occasionally tunnels and the readout makes mistakes. The ratio of Zeeman energy to thermal energy is therefore one of the first things a readout depends on (Chapter 15).
  • Readout limits everything after it. Once the readout works, every later experiment is "do something, then read out". If the readout misidentifies the state 10% of the time, every Rabi oscillation, every Ramsey fringe and every benchmarking curve has its contrast reduced, and you need more repetitions to see the same thing. Groups therefore invest heavily in readout before doing anything ambitious with the qubit.

1.4Energy scales decide what is possible

Almost every design decision and every tuning step in this field comes down to comparing energies. A qubit works only if certain energies are well separated from each other. Figure 1.3 places the important ones for our device on one logarithmic axis.

Read the ladder from the bottom up, and each rung has a job:

  • The charging energy (millielectronvolts) is the cost of adding one more electron to a dot. Because it is so large, the number of electrons on a dot is a sharp integer that stays put unless you deliberately change it.
  • The orbital spacing (about 3 meV) keeps the electron in its lowest orbital, so the dot behaves like a simple two-level spin system and not a little atom with many states.
  • The valley splitting (100 to 300 µeV in good silicon devices) is specific to silicon. Silicon's conduction band has two nearly degenerate minima, or valleys, along the growth direction. The interface lifts this degeneracy, but only by a small and device-dependent amount. If the valley splitting is not comfortably larger than the Zeeman energy and the thermal energy, a second set of states joins the party and spoils both readout and coherence (Chapter 14).
  • The Zeeman energy (64 µeV at 0.55 T) is the qubit itself: the energy between spin down and spin up. It must be large compared with the thermal energy so that the spin can be initialized and read out, and small compared with the valley and orbital energies so that the qubit stays a clean two-level system.
  • The thermal energy kBT at an electron temperature of 50 mK is about 4.3 µeV. Every readout scheme needs it to be well below the energies it relies on.
  • The control energies, the Rabi frequency and the exchange coupling, are a million times smaller than the charging energy. Small control energies mean gentle, precise rotations. The price is that the rotations take tens to hundreds of nanoseconds, which must be short compared with the coherence times.

Keep this ladder in mind. Whenever a tuning step looks mysterious, the reason is almost always one of these comparisons.

1.5Time scales decide how fast you can work

The second ladder is in time (Figure 1.4). It tells you two things: which operations fit inside which coherence time, and how long an experiment takes to acquire.

The bottom of the ladder is physics: a gate takes about 100 ns, the spin dephases in microseconds when left alone, and an echo extends that to tens or hundreds of microseconds. The top of the ladder is life in the lab: the device drifts over minutes to hours, so calibrations must be repeated, and a cooldown takes days, so you do not warm up casually.

The middle of the ladder, the readout, decides how fast you learn. Each data point in a qubit experiment is a probability, estimated by repeating the same sequence many times. How long one repetition takes is set mostly by the readout and by how long you wait for the spin to reset.

Worked numbers: how long does a Rabi chevron take?

A standard early experiment, the Rabi chevron (Chapter 19), scans the microwave frequency over 100 values and the burst duration over 100 values. That is 10,000 points, each repeated 200 times to estimate a probability: 2 million shots.

With Elzerman readout (Chapter 15) a shot takes about 1 ms: a few hundred microseconds to load and initialize, the pulse itself, and a readout window of a few hundred microseconds. Two million shots × 1 ms = 2000 s, about 33 minutes.

With Pauli-blockade readout and fast reflectometry (Chapter 16), a shot can take 20 µs. Two million shots × 20 µs = 40 s.

The same measurement is 50 times faster. Over a week of calibrations, that difference decides whether you can afford to recalibrate every hour. This is why so much effort goes into faster readout.

1.6What a single data point really is

A qubit measurement gives one bit: up or down. A probability such as "the spin-up probability after this pulse" is estimated by repeating the experiment N times and counting. The estimate has a statistical uncertainty set by the binomial distribution,

\[ \sigma_P = \sqrt{\frac{P(1-P)}{N}}, \]

which is largest at P = 0.5. With N = 200 shots, σ is about 3.5% at P = 0.5, and halving it needs four times as many shots. This is why experiments are planned around the shot count, and why a fast readout is worth so much: precision costs time, and the cost grows as the square of the precision you want.

The measured probability is also not the true one. If the readout misidentifies spin down as spin up with probability α and spin up as spin down with probability β, the probability you record is

\[ P_{\text{meas}} = \alpha + (1 - \alpha - \beta)\,P_{\text{true}}. \]

The factor 1 − α − β is the visibility. A Rabi oscillation that should swing from 0 to 1 instead swings from α to 1 − β. A visibility of 0.7, common in older experiments, means every oscillation is squeezed into 70% of its full range. Chapter 17 shows how to measure α and β honestly, and Chapter 23 how benchmarking protocols are designed to be insensitive to them.

1.7How long it really takes

It helps to know roughly how a campaign unfolds in calendar time. The durations below are typical for a group with an established fabrication process and a working setup. A first device of a new design, or a new lab, can spend months at the early stages; a mature group with reproducible devices can go from cooldown to a calibrated qubit in a week or two.

StageTypical durationWhat usually takes the time
Mounting, bonding, cooldown2 to 4 daysCareful bonding; 1 to 2 days of cooling; checking every line once cold
Signs of life1 to 3 daysFinding which gates work, mapping turn-on and pinch-off, first Coulomb peaks
Sensor and reflectometry2 days to 2 weeksTuning a sensitive sensor dot; matching the tank circuit
Few-electron double dot1 to 3 weeksReaching the last electron in both dots; stable virtual gates; tunnel rates in range
Spin readoutdays to 2 weeksFinding the readout point, optimizing tunnel rates and thresholds
First qubit and coherencedaysSearching for the resonance in frequency; then routine Rabi, Ramsey, echo
Calibrated, benchmarked gates1 to 4 weeksPulse calibration, drift, heating effects, crosstalk
Two-qubit gatesweeks to monthsExchange control, symmetric operation, phase corrections, benchmarking

Something always goes wrong, so these durations include a realistic amount of debugging. One of the purposes of the "When it goes wrong" boxes in this book is to shorten that part.

1.8The device passport

Throughout the book we collect what we learn about our device in a single table, which we call its passport. Labs keep the same thing under various names: a parameter file, a "variable manager", a calibration database. The QuTech six-qubit processor, for example, kept 108 calibrated parameters in such a record and refreshed parts of it every morning [6]. Here is the passport before anything has been measured, with only the design values we expect:

Check yourself

1. A colleague proposes searching for the spin resonance before the charge sensor is tuned, "to save time". Why will this not work?

Show answer
Finding the resonance means applying microwaves and checking whether the spin flipped. The only way to see a spin flip is through spin-to-charge conversion, which needs a working charge sensor and a dot with one electron and known tunnel rates. Without the readout there is no signal, so the search cannot tell when it hits the resonance.

2. Using 1 µeV ↔ 11.6 mK, what electron temperature would make the thermal energy equal to one tenth of a 64 µeV Zeeman splitting? Is that easy to reach?

Show answer
One tenth of 64 µeV is 6.4 µeV, which corresponds to 6.4 × 11.6 ≈ 74 mK. Electron temperatures of 40 to 100 mK are common in well-filtered dilution refrigerators, so this is achievable but not automatic. It depends on filtering and thermalization (Chapter 4).

3. A Ramsey scan has 80 delay values and you want ±2.5% uncertainty at P = 0.5. How many shots per point, and how long does the scan take with 1 ms shots?

Show answer
σ = √(0.25/N) = 0.025 gives N = 0.25/0.000625 = 400 shots. 80 × 400 = 32,000 shots, which is 32 s at 1 ms per shot.

Part A · The whole picture · Chapter 2

The device we will follow

Every tuning step later in this book makes sense once you can picture what is underneath the gates: where the electrons live, what each gate pulls on, and what the micromagnet adds. This chapter builds that picture for our device, a silicon double quantum dot with a charge sensor and a micromagnet, and then contrasts it with the GaAs devices the field started with.

2.1The idea in one paragraph

A quantum dot is a puddle of electrons small enough that adding one more costs a large, well-defined energy. To make one, you need three things: a place where electrons can live in two dimensions, a way to confine them laterally to a region tens of nanometres across, and a way to control how many electrons are inside and how easily they tunnel in and out. In our device the first is a thin silicon layer buried in silicon–germanium. The second and third are provided by metal gates on the surface, whose voltages shape the electrostatic potential underneath. A larger dot next to the qubits acts as a sensitive electrometer that can see a single electron arrive or leave. A strip of cobalt on top makes a magnetic field that varies in space, which is what lets an oscillating electric field rotate the spin.

2.2The heterostructure: a quiet place for electrons

Figure 2.1 shows the layers. Read it from the bottom up, because that is the order in which they are grown.

The silicon wafer at the bottom is just a support. Silicon and germanium have lattice constants that differ by about 4%, so a germanium-rich layer cannot be grown directly on silicon without defects. Instead, the germanium fraction is increased gradually over a few micrometres (the graded buffer), so that the misfit dislocations form deep down and the top of the buffer is a relaxed Si0.7Ge0.3 crystal with its own, larger lattice constant.

The quantum well is a thin layer of pure silicon grown on top of that. It is forced to adopt the larger in-plane lattice constant of the SiGe beneath, so it is under tensile strain. Strain does something important for us. Bulk silicon has six equivalent conduction-band minima, or valleys, along ±x, ±y and ±z in momentum space. Tensile in-plane strain lowers the two valleys along the growth direction (±z) by much more than any energy we care about, so only those two matter. Those two are then split by the sharp interface into the valley splitting, which in Si/SiGe is typically tens to a few hundred µeV and varies from dot to dot. We will meet it again in Chapter 14; for now remember that silicon electrons carry this extra, small degree of freedom.

The SiGe on both sides of the well has a conduction band roughly 150 meV higher than the silicon, so electrons in the well are confined vertically to its 8 nm thickness. The confinement energy is tens of millielectronvolts, so vertically the electron is always in its ground state and the problem becomes two-dimensional.

The spacer above the well is the most important design choice in the stack. Its thickness, 30 nm here, sets how far the electrons sit from the surface and the gates. A thicker spacer keeps the electrons away from charge traps at the oxide interface, which reduces disorder and charge noise. But it also makes the gates' influence weaker and blurrier: lever arms shrink, and the dots cannot be squeezed as tightly. Most modern Si/SiGe qubit devices use spacers of 30 to 60 nm [6, 7, 8].

Two things are deliberately missing from this stack. First, there are no dopants. Older Si/SiGe devices had a layer of donors in the SiGe that supplied the electrons, but the ionized donors were a major source of charge noise and instability. Our device is undoped: no electrons are present until a gate pulls them in from the ohmic contacts [8]. Second, the silicon in the well is isotopically purified. Natural silicon contains 4.7% 29Si, whose nucleus has spin 1/2. An electron in a dot spreads over roughly a million silicon atoms, about forty thousand of which are 29Si. Their randomly oriented nuclear spins add up to a fluctuating magnetic field of about 10 µT, which dephases the qubit in about a microsecond [9]. Growing the well from purified 28Si (residual 29Si around 800 ppm, or 0.08%) removes most of this effect and lengthens the dephasing time by an order of magnitude [10].

2.3Where the electrons come from

Electrons enter through ohmic contacts: regions near the edge of the device that are implanted with phosphorus so heavily that they conduct like a metal even at millikelvin temperatures. Each ohmic is wired to the outside world. Between the ohmics and the dots, large lead gates (also called reservoir or accumulation gates) are biased positive enough to accumulate a two-dimensional electron gas, a "sea" of electrons with a well-defined Fermi level. These seas are the reservoirs that the dots exchange electrons with, and they are what the ohmic contacts connect to.

So the electrical path into a dot is: room-temperature wire → filters → ohmic contact → reservoir under a lead gate → tunnel barrier under a barrier gate → the dot. Every link in that chain can fail, and the first cooldown checks them one by one (Chapter 6).

2.4The gates and what each one does

Figure 2.3 shows the gate layout from above. The design follows the overlapping-gate architecture introduced by Princeton and HRL, in which several layers of metal gates, separated by a few nanometres of aluminium oxide, overlap so that each gate's tip sits exactly where it is needed [7, 8].

Each type of gate has one main job:

  • Plunger gates (P1, P2) sit directly above the dots. Raising a plunger's voltage lowers the potential energy of an electron in the dot below it, which pulls the dot's levels down and eventually lets another electron in. The plunger is the "how many electrons" knob.
  • Barrier gates (B1, B2, B3) sit between dots, or between a dot and a reservoir. Raising a barrier's voltage lowers the potential hill between two regions and makes tunnelling easier. B1 and B3 set how fast each dot exchanges electrons with its reservoir; B2 sets the tunnel coupling between the two dots, and therefore, later, the exchange interaction between the two spins (Chapter 24). Tunnel rates depend exponentially on the barrier voltage: a few millivolts change them by a factor of ten. HRL reported controlling a dot–reservoir rate over nine orders of magnitude with one barrier gate [8].
  • Screening gates (CS) are in the lowest layer and are held at a low or slightly negative voltage. They stop the plungers' leads, which must cross over the device to reach the dots, from accumulating electrons along their whole length, so electrons gather only under the gate tips. They also define the narrow channel in which the dot array sits.
  • Lead gates (LL, LR, SL, SR) accumulate the reservoirs over the ohmic contacts. They are usually set once and left alone.

Because each gate sits on a different layer, the tips can be placed tens of nanometres apart, and each gate is much closer to "its" feature than to anything else. That is the point of the overlapping design. In older single-layer depletion-mode devices, several gates had comparable influence on each dot. In the overlapping design the largest unwanted coupling is typically 20 to 30% [8]. Not zero, which is why virtual gates exist (Chapter 11), but small enough that tuning is manageable.

The gate metal is aluminium or a titanium–palladium bilayer, a few tens of nanometres thick. Between layers there is a few nanometres of aluminium oxide grown by atomic layer deposition, and the same oxide separates the lowest gates from the semiconductor. This oxide matters more than it seems. It contains defects that can trap and release charges, and these fluctuating charges are one of the main sources of the charge noise that ultimately limits qubit coherence. Rochester measured noticeably more charge noise in devices with thicker oxide [11].

2.5The charge sensor

Below the qubit dots, a second channel holds the sensor dot SD, with its own plunger SP, barriers SB1 and SB2, and reservoirs connected to ohmics O3 and O4. It is a full single-electron transistor in its own right: current can flow from O3 through SD to O4, but only when one of SD's levels lines up with the reservoirs.

The trick that makes it a sensor is electrostatic. The sensor dot is close enough to the qubit dots that an electron entering D2 shifts SD's levels slightly, as if someone had nudged SP. If SD is tuned to the steep side of a conductance peak, that small shift produces a large change in current. In our device one electron on D2 shifts the sensor peak by roughly half its width, enough to see a single tunnelling event in a few microseconds once the sensor is read out with radio-frequency reflectometry (Chapters 9 and 10). The sensor's coupling falls off quickly with distance, roughly as the inverse cube in densely gated devices, because the metal gates screen it [7]. That is why sensors must sit within a dot pitch or two of the qubits.

2.6The micromagnet

The last ingredient is magnetic. A uniform external field B₀ splits the spin states and sets the qubit frequency, but a uniform field cannot be used to rotate one spin without rotating all of them. The micromagnet solves both problems at once.

It is a layer of cobalt about 200 nm thick, patterned on top of the gate stack. When the external field is applied in the plane of the device (0.40 T in our case), the cobalt magnetizes along it and produces its own stray field at the dots, about 0.15 T. That stray field has two parts that do different jobs (Figure 2.4):

  • The longitudinal component B∥ points along B₀ and simply adds to it. Because it is different at the two dots, the two spins have different Zeeman energies and therefore different resonance frequencies. A microwave tone at one qubit's frequency rotates only that qubit. This is how individual spins are addressed with a shared drive line.
  • The transverse component B⊥ points perpendicular to B₀ and changes with position. An oscillating voltage on a gate pushes the electron back and forth by a fraction of a nanometre. In a transverse gradient, that motion makes the electron feel an oscillating transverse magnetic field, which is exactly what drives spin resonance. This is electric-dipole spin resonance (EDSR) with a "slanting" field [12, 13].

The gradients are a double-edged sword, and this trade-off runs through the rest of the book. The transverse gradient makes driving fast. The longitudinal gradient makes the qubits addressable, but it also means that if the electron moves, its frequency changes. Charge noise jiggles every electron by picometres all the time, so a longitudinal gradient turns charge noise into frequency noise, and therefore into dephasing. RIKEN designed their magnet to keep the longitudinal gradient near 0.2 mT/nm for exactly this reason, and found that in purified silicon this was then what limited the coherence [10]. Micromagnet design is a careful compromise [14, 15].

Worked numbers: from field to frequency

For a free electron in silicon, g ≈ 2, so the Zeeman frequency is f = gμBB/h ≈ 28.0 GHz/T × B.

At dot 1 the total field is approximately B₀ + B∥ = 0.40 + 0.148 T, plus a small perpendicular part of 0.093 T that adds in quadrature: |B| = √(0.548² + 0.093²) ≈ 0.556 T, giving f ≈ 15.6 GHz.

At dot 2 the simulation gives B∥ = 0.171 T and B⊥ = 0.063 T, so |B| ≈ 0.575 T and f ≈ 16.1 GHz. The predicted difference is about 0.5 GHz.

When we measure the real device in Chapter 18, the two qubits will be at 15.42 and 15.72 GHz: close to the prediction, but not equal to it. This is normal. Dots never sit exactly where the design puts them, and the magnet is never perfectly saturated or perfectly shaped. In the QuTech six-qubit device, the measured qubit frequencies did not follow the simulated spacing either [6]. Simulations tell you the scale; only spectroscopy tells you the actual frequencies.

One practical consequence: the micromagnet only works properly once it is magnetized close to saturation, which for these cobalt structures takes an in-plane field of a few tenths of a tesla. That is one reason Si/SiGe micromagnet devices typically run at B₀ = 0.3 to 0.7 T, with qubit frequencies of 10 to 20 GHz [9, 10, 16, 17]. The field is ramped once, slowly, and then left alone.

2.7The GaAs device, for contrast

Spin qubits were born in gallium arsenide, and many of the techniques in this book were invented there [1]. A typical GaAs device looks superficially similar but works in the opposite way:

PropertyOur Si/SiGe deviceTypical GaAs/AlGaAs deviceConsequence
Where electrons come fromAccumulated by positive gates from implanted ohmics (undoped)Already present: a doped AlGaAs layer supplies a 2DEG at zero gate voltageGaAs gates are negative and deplete; Si gates are positive and accumulate
Effective mass0.19 me0.067 meGaAs dots can be larger for the same orbital spacing, so lithography is easier
g-factor≈ 2 (28 GHz/T)≈ −0.44 (6.2 GHz/T)GaAs needs several tesla for the same Zeeman energy
Nuclear spinsFew (0.08% 29Si after purification)Every Ga and As nucleus has spinGaAs spins dephase in ~10–20 ns unless the nuclei are controlled
ValleysTwo low valleys, split by 10s–100s µeVNone (single Γ-point minimum)Valley physics is a silicon-specific complication
Spin–orbit couplingWeakModerateGaAs spins can be driven without a micromagnet, but relax faster

The comparison explains the history. GaAs heterostructures were cleaner and easier to gate, so the first single-spin readout [18], the first coherent exchange oscillations [19] and the first EDSR [20] were all done in GaAs. But the nuclear spins limited coherence so severely that the field moved to silicon once silicon devices became clean enough [2, 3]. GaAs remains a valuable teaching and research platform, and Chapter 27 uses it to explain singlet–triplet qubits in their original setting.

Two other platforms deserve a mention. Si-MOS devices put the electrons directly at a Si/SiO₂ interface under the gates, with no SiGe spacer. Lever arms are larger and valley splittings are often larger, but the electrons sit right next to the oxide's defects. Germanium hole devices confine holes rather than electrons in a strained Ge well. Holes have strong spin–orbit coupling, so they can be driven electrically without any micromagnet, and they have no valleys [21, 22]. Chapter 29 covers them.

2.8What can be wrong with a device before you start

A finished chip is the result of dozens of fabrication steps, and not every device on a chip works. Knowing the common failure modes helps you interpret the first measurements:

  • Broken or shorted gates. A gate line can be interrupted where it crosses a step in the layer below, or two layers can short through a pinhole in the oxide. The first electrical checks find these (Chapters 3 and 6).
  • Gate leakage. Weak oxide lets current flow from a gate into the semiconductor at high voltages. A leaky gate is noisy and must be kept below its leakage onset.
  • Bad ohmics. An ohmic contact that does not reach the well is an open circuit, and the reservoir it should feed is unusable.
  • Disorder. Trapped charges near the interface can create unintended dots or block the channel. Disorder shows up as irregular, non-periodic Coulomb peaks and charge transitions that cannot be attributed to any intended dot.
  • Small valley splitting. Not visible until spin experiments begin, and not fixable by tuning beyond a modest range. It is a property of the interface at the dot's location [23].

The next three chapters take the chip from the box to the bottom of the fridge, and Chapter 6 starts checking for all of these.

Check yourself

1. In our device, what happens if every gate is left at 0 V?

Show answer
Nothing conducts. The heterostructure is undoped, so with no positive voltage on the lead gates there is no electron gas, and the ohmic contacts are not connected to anything. This is why the first cooldown measurements start by turning on the lead gates (Chapter 6).

2. Why does a thicker SiGe spacer reduce charge noise but make tuning harder?

Show answer
Charge noise comes largely from traps near the oxide and the surface. A thicker spacer puts the electrons farther from them, so their fluctuating fields are weaker at the dot. But the gates are also farther away, so each gate's potential is more spread out: lever arms are smaller, cross-coupling between gates is larger, and it is harder to make small, well-separated dots.

3. A colleague says the micromagnet's longitudinal gradient is "pure benefit" because it gives addressability. What is the hidden cost?

Show answer
A longitudinal gradient makes the qubit frequency depend on the electron's position. Charge noise moves the electron by tiny amounts, so the gradient converts charge noise into qubit frequency noise, which causes dephasing. In purified silicon this can become the dominant dephasing mechanism, so the gradient must be large enough to separate the qubits but no larger.

Part B · Getting a chip ready and cold · Chapter 3

From chip to sample holder

Between receiving a chip and closing the fridge lies a day or two of careful, unglamorous work: looking at the device, checking that its gates are intact, gluing and bonding it to a circuit board, and connecting that board to the fridge wiring. Mistakes at this stage are expensive, because you only discover them after a multi-day cooldown, and some of them destroy the device outright. This chapter explains what is done, and what each step protects against.

3.1Look before you touch

A chip usually carries several devices, some nominally identical, some variations of the design. Before choosing which one to measure, every candidate is inspected under an optical microscope. With 50× to 100× objectives you can see the gate pattern clearly, though not the finest features. You are looking for anything that would make the device fail:

  • Interrupted gate lines. A gate in an upper layer must climb over the edges of the layers below. If the metal is too thin at such a step it can crack, leaving the tip of the gate disconnected from its bond pad. On an optical image this shows up as a thin dark line or a missing segment.
  • Lift-off residue. Gates are defined by depositing metal through a patterned resist and dissolving the resist ("lift-off"). Imperfect lift-off leaves flakes or "flags" of metal that can short neighbouring gates.
  • Misalignment between layers. The layers are written in separate lithography steps. If one layer is shifted by 20 nm, plungers and barriers no longer sit where the design assumes, and the device may still work but will tune differently.
  • The micromagnet. Is it present, complete, and still attached? Cobalt can peel if adhesion is poor.

The finest features (gate tips 30 to 50 nm wide) are only visible in a scanning electron microscope. Groups usually image a sister device, not the one they will measure, because the electron beam deposits charge and contamination and can damage thin oxides. The SEM images in published papers are almost always captioned "a device nominally identical to the one measured" for exactly this reason [6, 7].

3.2Static electricity: the invisible way to destroy a device

The gates sit on a few nanometres of oxide, and different gate layers are separated by similar thicknesses. Aluminium oxide breaks down at fields of very roughly 0.5 to 1 V/nm, so a few volts across a thin layer is enough to punch a permanent conducting hole through it. A person walking across a floor can charge up to several thousand volts. Touching a gate pad, or a cable connected to one, discharges that through the oxide in nanoseconds. The device is usually ruined without any visible damage.

Every lab therefore treats devices as if they were the most static-sensitive components in the building. The standard precautions:

  • A grounded wrist strap and a grounded antistatic mat whenever you handle the chip, the sample board, or any cable that will connect to it.
  • All lines of the device shorted together and to ground whenever it is not being measured. Sample boards and breakout boxes have switches or shorting plugs for this. The rule is simple: ground before you disconnect, connect before you unground.
  • Ionizing air blowers near the bonder and microscope, especially in dry winter air.
  • Instruments connected to the device turned on, set to 0 V, and grounded before the device lines are released from ground.
When it goes wrong

What you see: at the first cold measurement, one gate draws current as soon as it is raised by a few hundred millivolts, or two gates behave as if they were one.

Likely cause: oxide breakdown, often from an electrostatic discharge during bonding or connection, or from a voltage step applied without a slow ramp.

What to do: map exactly which pairs are shorted (Chapter 6). A gate shorted to the semiconductor can sometimes be left floating or grounded while the rest of the device is used. A short between two gates can sometimes be lived with if they would be set to similar voltages. Then review the handling procedure, because it will happen again.

3.3Room-temperature electrical checks

Before bonding, some groups test the device on a probe station: fine needles placed on the bond pads, connected to a source-measure unit with a strict current limit. Others do the same test after bonding, through the sample board. Either way, the goal is to catch shorts before investing a cooldown.

The useful tests at room temperature are about isolation. Each gate should be isolated from every other gate and from the ohmic contacts by much more than 1 GΩ: applying 0.5 V should produce no measurable current, below about 100 pA. Voltages stay small (well below 1 V), are ramped slowly, and every lead is grounded before and after. A gate that already leaks at room temperature will not get better when cold.

Two other room-temperature measurements are much less informative than they look. At room temperature, an undoped Si/SiGe device has no two-dimensional electron gas, so the resistance between two ohmics tells you little about whether they will contact the well when cold. In GaAs, where the doped 2DEG exists at room temperature, a two-terminal ohmic-to-ohmic resistance of a few to tens of kilohms is a reasonable sign of life. Gate continuity also cannot easily be tested with a DC meter, because a gate is a single wire with one pad, ending in an open tip. A broken gate looks electrically identical to an intact one until it is cold and fails to pinch off (Chapter 7).

3.4Gluing and bonding

The chip is fixed to the sample printed circuit board (PCB), or to a chip carrier that plugs into one. The glue must hold at millikelvin temperatures and conduct heat; silver epoxy, GE varnish and PMMA are all used. QuTech, for example, glues the chip with PMMA to the gold-plated copper ground plane of the board [24]. What matters is that the chip is well thermally anchored. An electron gas that is poorly coupled to the cold plate runs hotter, and the electron temperature limits spin readout (Chapter 15).

Each bond pad on the chip is then connected to a pad on the board with a wire bond: a 25 µm aluminium wire welded at both ends by ultrasonic energy. A device like ours needs 20 to 40 bonds. Three details matter:

  • Order. Bond ground connections first, then the ohmics, then the gates, with all board lines grounded throughout. The bonder itself must be grounded, and the ultrasonic pulse should be gentle on gate pads, which sit on thin oxide.
  • Length on fast lines. A bond wire has an inductance of roughly 1 nH per millimetre. At 15 GHz, 1 nH has a reactance of 2π × 15 GHz × 1 nH ≈ 94 Ω, larger than the 50 Ω impedance of the line. A long bond on the microwave gate reflects and attenuates the drive; it also radiates. Microwave and fast-pulse lines get the shortest possible bonds, sometimes two or three in parallel.
  • Record. Draw or photograph the bond map: which chip pad goes to which board line. Months later, when a gate misbehaves, this map is the first thing you will want.

3.5The sample board: where the experiment begins

The sample PCB is not just a passive adapter. It carries the last stage of filtering for the DC lines, the bias tees that let fast pulses and DC voltages share a gate, and the inductor that turns the sensor into a radio-frequency resonator. Figure 3.1 shows the four kinds of connection our device needs.

DC lines and their last filter

Most gates only ever need slowly varying voltages. Their lines arrive as filtered twisted pairs from the fridge (Chapter 4), and the board adds one more RC low-pass stage right next to the chip. The point of filtering so close to the device is that anything picked up between the last filter and the gate, such as radiation inside the sample enclosure, is not filtered at all. A cutoff of a kilohertz or so is typical for gates that are only swept slowly. It is low enough to remove almost everything, and high enough that slow sweeps are not distorted.

Bias tees on fast gates

The plungers and the interdot barrier need two things at once: a stable DC voltage that sets their operating point, and fast pulses (nanoseconds to milliseconds) that move the dots between initialization, manipulation and readout. A bias tee combines them. The DC voltage arrives through a large resistor R, the pulses through a capacitor C, and the gate sees their sum.

The price is that the pulse path is high-pass filtered, with time constant RC. A square pulse that lasts longer than a small fraction of RC visibly sags, because the capacitor slowly charges and the pulse amplitude decays towards zero. This is why on-board bias tees use very long time constants.

Worked numbers: how much does a pulse droop?

With R = 2 MΩ and C = 100 nF, the time constant is RC = 0.2 s and the high-pass corner is fc = 1/(2πRC) ≈ 0.8 Hz.

A rectangular pulse of duration τ held through the bias tee decays as e−τ/RC. For a 1 ms readout-level pulse the amplitude drops by τ/RC = 1 ms / 0.2 s = 0.5%. On a 10 mV pulse that is 50 µV, which corresponds to a 5 µeV shift of a dot level at a lever arm of 0.1 eV/V. That is about one thermal energy, which is enough to matter for spin readout. Long sequences therefore keep the average voltage of each pulse cycle close to zero (they are "compensated"), and the readout point is calibrated with the pulse sequence running, not in DC.

Bias tees also shape fast edges. The capacitor, the bond wires and the on-chip gate lines all filter and reflect high frequencies, so a pulse that leaves the generator with a 1 ns edge may arrive at the dot rounded and with ripples. Chapter 13 shows how these distortions are measured on the device itself and pre-compensated [25].

The microwave line

For EDSR, a 10 to 20 GHz signal must reach one gate with as little loss and reflection as possible. On the board it travels on a 50 Ω coplanar waveguide right to the chip edge, and the final bond is kept short. In our device the microwaves are applied to plunger P1, so P1's line must carry both microwaves and fast pulses. This is done with a broadband bias tee or a dedicated combining network. Some designs instead have a separate microwave gate or an on-chip antenna.

The tank circuit

The sensor dot will be read out with radio-frequency reflectometry, which needs the sensor's resistance to be part of a resonant circuit (Chapter 10). On our board the sensor's source ohmic O3 is connected through a surface-mount inductor of 1.2 µH. The other element of the resonator is the parasitic capacitance of the board trace, the bond pad and the bond wire to ground, about 0.5 pF. Together they resonate near

\[ f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC_p}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{1.2\ \mu\text{H} \times 0.5\ \text{pF}}} \approx 205\ \text{MHz}. \]

Because the parasitic capacitance is set by the layout and the bonds, it can only be estimated before cooldown. The real resonance frequency is measured cold, and it typically differs from the estimate by 10 to 20%.

3.6Into the fridge

The board, with the chip bonded and all lines grounded, is mounted on the cold finger of the dilution refrigerator: a gold-plated copper rod or plate bolted to the mixing-chamber stage. A copper or brass enclosure usually surrounds the board to block thermal radiation and stray microwaves. Before the enclosure is closed, a few things deserve care:

  • Orientation in the magnet. Our qubits need an in-plane field along the micromagnet's intended magnetization direction. The board is mounted so that the device axes line up with the magnet's axes, and the angle is written down. In silicon, the field direction relative to the crystal axes also changes the g-factor slightly through spin–orbit effects [26], so a well-documented orientation saves confusion later.
  • Line checks through the fridge wiring. With the device still grounded at the board, measure each line from the room-temperature breakout box. Every DC line should show the expected series resistance of its wiring and filters (often a few hundred ohms to a few kilohms), and no line should be shorted to another. Each coax should be checked for continuity.
  • Photos and notes. A photograph of the mounted board, the bond map and the line assignment go into the lab notebook before the radiation shields go on.

Check yourself

1. Why is the last RC filter placed on the sample board rather than at room temperature, where it would be easier to change?

Show answer
Any noise or radiation coupled into the line after the last filter reaches the gate unfiltered. Filtering right next to the chip removes what is picked up along the way, including inside the fridge and the sample enclosure. Filters at room temperature also cannot remove the thermal noise of the warmer parts of the wiring.

2. A readout pulse of 3 mV is held for 5 ms through a bias tee with RC = 50 ms. How far does it sag by the end, and what does that mean in energy for a lever arm of 0.1 eV/V?

Show answer
The fractional sag is about τ/RC = 5/50 = 10%, i.e. 0.3 mV. Times 0.1 eV/V that is 30 µeV, about half the Zeeman energy of our qubit. That is far too much for spin readout, which needs the level placement to be stable to a few µeV. This bias tee is not suitable for such long pulses.

3. Why do published papers so often show an SEM image of a device "nominally identical" to the one measured?

Show answer
Imaging with an electron beam deposits charge and carbon contamination and can damage thin oxides. Labs therefore avoid imaging the device they will measure, and image a sister device fabricated in the same run instead.

Part B · Getting a chip ready and cold · Chapter 4

The fridge as part of the experiment

A dilution refrigerator can cool its coldest plate to 10 mK, but the electrons in a device on that plate are usually several times hotter. Whether they end up at 40 mK or at 200 mK depends almost entirely on how the wires reaching them are filtered, attenuated and thermally anchored. Since spin readout depends directly on electron temperature, the fridge wiring is really the first part of the experiment.

4.1How the fridge gets cold

Modern "dry" dilution refrigerators need no liquid helium bath. Their cooling happens in stages, each a metal plate held at a fixed temperature, with the experiment hanging below the coldest one:

StageTemperatureWhat cools itTypical cooling power
50 K plate40–60 Kfirst stage of the pulse-tube cryocoolertens of watts
4 K plate3–4 Ksecond stage of the pulse tubeabout 1 W
Still0.7–0.9 Kevaporation of ³He from the dilute phasetens of mW
Cold plate≈ 100 mKthe outgoing ³He stream (heat exchangers)sub-mW
Mixing chamber (MXC)8–20 mK³He crossing from the concentrated to the dilute phase≈ 10–20 µW at 20 mK, hundreds of µW at 100 mK

The physics of the last stage is worth a sentence, because it is often described wrongly. Below about 0.8 K, a mixture of ³He and ⁴He separates into two liquid phases: one almost pure ³He (the concentrated phase) floating on one with about 6% ³He dissolved in superfluid ⁴He (the dilute phase). Moving a ³He atom from the concentrated phase into the dilute phase absorbs heat, much as evaporation does. This happens at the phase boundary in the mixing chamber, which is where the cooling is produced. The still supplies the driving force. It is heated to evaporate ³He preferentially from the dilute phase, which is then pumped away, recondensed and returned to the concentrated phase. The circulation of ³He through this loop produces the cooling, and the still heater sets how fast it circulates.

Cooling from room temperature to base takes one to two days for a typical system. The outer vacuum can is pumped, the pulse tube cools everything to about 4 K over roughly a day, then the mixture is condensed and circulation started. Warming up takes a similar time, so a cooldown is a commitment: whatever is wrong with the wiring or the bonding stays wrong for days.

4.2Why the electrons are hotter than the fridge

The electrons in the device's reservoirs exchange heat with two things: the crystal lattice, through electron–phonon scattering, and the outside world, through the wires connected to them. At millikelvin temperatures the electron–phonon coupling is extremely weak; the heat flow it can carry falls roughly as T⁵. The wires, meanwhile, carry noise: the thermal (Johnson) noise of every warm resistor along the way, radiation leaking down coaxial cables, and interference picked up from the lab. A tiny noise power, picowatts or less, is enough to keep the electrons well above the lattice temperature.

The result is that the electron temperature Te, the temperature that appears in the Fermi function of the reservoirs, is usually 30 to 150 mK even with the mixing chamber at 10 mK. In Si/SiGe single-shot readout experiments, values around 100 to 200 mK were common for years. Princeton reported about 45 mK by thermalizing the device carefully at the mixing chamber and eliminating ground loops, which was what made more than 99% readout visibility possible [27].

Figure 4.1 shows why this matters so much. During spin readout (Chapter 15) the two spin levels of the dot are placed on either side of the reservoir's Fermi level. Only the upper (spin-up) electron should be able to tunnel out, into the empty states above the Fermi level. But the Fermi distribution is not a sharp step. At finite temperature some states below the Fermi level are also empty, so the spin-down electron has a small probability of leaving too, and that is counted as a wrong answer.

The relevant number is the ratio of Zeeman energy to thermal energy. For our qubit, EZ/kBTe ≈ 64 µeV / 4.3 µeV ≈ 15 at 50 mK, but only ≈ 3.7 at 200 mK. Keith and co-workers showed that Elzerman readout with 99% visibility requires EZ ≳ 13 kBTe [28, 27]. You can raise EZ with a larger magnetic field, but that costs you elsewhere: shorter T1, higher microwave frequencies, more heating. Lowering Te is the better route, and it is mostly decided by the wiring.

4.3DC lines: slow on purpose

Most of the device's lines carry slowly varying gate voltages and source–drain biases. They are made of thin twisted pairs of resistive alloy wire (phosphor bronze, manganin or constantan) above 4 K, and often superconducting NbTi below. Resistive alloys are chosen because they conduct heat poorly: a copper wire from room temperature would carry far too much heat to the cold stages. Each wire is thermally anchored at every plate, by wrapping it around a copper post or gluing it to a copper bobbin, so that it arrives at each stage already at that stage's temperature.

The lines are also filtered, in several stages, because noise at different frequencies needs different filters:

  • Low-pass RC filters (at room temperature, at the mixing chamber, and on the sample board) remove everything from audio frequencies upwards. A cutoff of 1 to 100 kHz is typical. These filters only work up to a few hundred megahertz, because their components stop behaving ideally at high frequencies.
  • Microwave-absorbing filters (metal-powder or Eccosorb filters, or meandering lossy lines) at the mixing chamber attenuate everything from about 100 MHz to tens of gigahertz by 50 dB or more. They stop thermal photons and radiation that would otherwise travel down the wires and heat the electrons, or excite the qubit directly.

The consequence is that a DC line is slow: a step applied at room temperature arrives at the gate smeared over tens of microseconds to milliseconds. That is fine for setting operating points and for slow sweeps, but any gate that must be pulsed quickly needs a separate coaxial line and a bias tee (Chapter 3).

4.4Coaxial lines and attenuators

Fast pulses, microwaves and the reflectometry carrier travel on coaxial cables. A coaxial cable from room temperature carries not only your signal but also the thermal noise of the 300 K electronics at its top, with a noise temperature of 300 K. If nothing is done, that noise arrives at the device and corresponds to hundreds of thermal photons per mode at 15 GHz.

The standard remedy is a chain of attenuators, each bolted to a stage. An attenuator of power ratio A at temperature Ts passes a fraction 1/A of the incoming noise and adds its own thermal noise in proportion to what it absorbs:

\[ T_{\text{out}} = \frac{T_{\text{in}}}{A} + T_s\left(1 - \frac{1}{A}\right). \]

Apply this stage by stage and the noise temperature falls to near the coldest stage's temperature, provided each stage has enough attenuation to suppress the noise from above (Figure 4.2).

Attenuation is not free, though. A pulse or microwave signal is attenuated by the same factor, so the room-temperature source must be stronger, and the power absorbed in each attenuator heats that stage. Spin-qubit experiments need fairly large signals. Plunger pulses are millivolts to tens of millivolts at the gate, and EDSR needs a few millivolts of microwave amplitude. Their lines therefore usually get less attenuation than the readout input, and the remaining noise is accepted. The balance between "enough attenuation to be cold" and "enough signal to work" is a standing design decision for every line.

Worked numbers: microwave power at the gate

Suppose EDSR needs a microwave amplitude of 2 mV at the gate. In a 50 Ω line the power is P = V²/(2Z₀) = (2 × 10⁻³)² / 100 = 4 × 10⁻⁸ W, which is 40 nW or −44 dBm.

The line has 40 dB of attenuators (Figure 4.3) plus about 10 dB of cable loss at 15 GHz, 50 dB in total. The source must therefore deliver −44 + 50 = +6 dBm, about 4 mW, at room temperature.

All but 40 nW of that is dissipated inside the fridge, mostly in the attenuators on the colder stages and in the cables. On the coldest stages, microwatts of heating are already significant. This is one reason long microwave bursts change the temperature of the device and shift the qubit frequency, an effect we will meet in Chapter 22 [24].

4.5The readout chain

The reflectometry readout (Chapter 10) needs two coaxial paths: one to send a weak radio-frequency carrier down to the tank circuit, and one to bring the reflected signal back up. Figure 4.3 shows how they are arranged.

Two features of this chain are easy to get wrong:

  • The directional coupler must be cold. The carrier comes down a heavily attenuated line, but the weak reflected signal must not go back up through those attenuators; it would lose 40 dB on the way. A directional coupler at the mixing chamber separates the two waves: the incoming carrier passes through to the tank, and the reflected wave is routed into a separate, low-loss output line towards the amplifier. At the 100 MHz to 1 GHz frequencies of reflectometry, cryogenic circulators are large and rarely used; directional couplers are the standard solution [5].
  • The amplifier must match the frequency. The first amplifier, a high-electron-mobility transistor (HEMT) amplifier at 4 K, sets the noise of the whole readout. Its noise temperature is a few kelvin, far below room-temperature amplifiers. It must be specified for the reflectometry band. An amplifier built for 4 to 8 GHz, common in superconducting-qubit setups, does nothing for a 200 MHz reflectometry signal. Some groups add a superconducting parametric amplifier at the mixing chamber to come closer to the quantum limit [29, 5].

The signal level involved is tiny. The carrier power at the tank is typically around −100 dBm (0.1 pW), because a larger carrier heats the sensor and broadens its Coulomb peaks (Chapter 10). After 35 to 40 dB of cryogenic gain and more at room temperature, the signal reaches the digitizer at a comfortable level.

4.6The magnet

The static field B₀ comes from a superconducting magnet around the sample space: a solenoid for one field direction, or a vector magnet with three orthogonal coils if the field direction must be varied. For our device the field is in plane along the micromagnet's magnetization axis, 0.40 T.

Superconducting magnets are ramped slowly (typically 0.05 to 0.2 T per minute near the sample) to avoid heating the fridge through eddy currents and to protect the magnet from quenching. Once at field, many magnets are switched into persistent mode: a superconducting switch closes across the coil, the current circulates without the power supply, and the supply can be ramped down. This removes the supply's current noise. But a persistent magnet slowly decays, by parts per million per hour, and at 15 GHz a decay of 1 ppm per hour shifts the qubit frequency by 15 kHz per hour. RIKEN recalibrated their qubit frequency roughly every hour for this reason [10].

One common misconception deserves correcting: magnetic shields of mu-metal or superconducting foil, standard for superconducting qubits, are not used around spin-qubit samples in a superconducting magnet. A high-permeability shield would saturate in a field of a few tenths of a tesla, and a superconducting shield would expel or trap the very field the experiment needs.

4.7Cooling down

With the shields closed and the device grounded at the breakout box, the cooldown itself is mostly automated. A few habits make it smoother:

  • Keep every device line grounded during the cooldown, and log the stage temperatures.
  • At 4 K, before condensing the mixture, check again that every line is continuous and isolated. Some faults (a cracked solder joint, a broken bond that has lifted) only appear when the board contracts, and they are much cheaper to find now than at base temperature.
  • Once at base, wait for the mixing chamber to settle before measuring anything temperature-sensitive. The device's own thermal anchoring may take hours to equilibrate.
When it goes wrong

What you see: charge transitions and Coulomb peaks are much broader than expected, and a Fermi-function fit gives Te of 150 to 300 mK although the mixing chamber is at 10 mK.

Likely causes, in rough order of frequency: ground loops between instruments (mains-frequency currents through the shields and wiring); insufficient high-frequency filtering on some line; a hot or noisy instrument connected to a gate; poor thermal anchoring of the chip; too large a sensor excitation, which heats the reservoirs [27].

What to do: measure the electron temperature from the width of a dot–reservoir transition (Chapter 8) while disconnecting instruments one by one, and while lowering the sensor excitation. A sudden improvement points to the culprit.

Check yourself

1. Your electron temperature is 120 mK and your Zeeman energy is 64 µeV. By how much would you need to raise the magnetic field to recover EZ = 15 kBTe? What would that cost?

Show answer
kBT at 120 mK is 10.3 µeV, so 15 kBT is 155 µeV, about 2.4 times the present Zeeman energy. The total field would have to go from 0.55 T to about 1.3 T, and the qubit frequency from 15.4 GHz to about 37 GHz. Microwave delivery at 37 GHz is much harder, heating grows, T1 typically shortens strongly at higher field, and the micromagnet gradients do not scale up. Lowering Te is almost always the better choice.

2. A line has 20 dB at 4 K and nothing else. What noise temperature reaches the device, and why is that a problem for a 15 GHz qubit?

Show answer
T = 300/100 + 4 × 0.99 ≈ 7 K. At 15.4 GHz, hf/kB ≈ 0.74 K, so the thermal photon number is 1/(e0.74/7 − 1) ≈ 9. That noise can drive spin transitions, heat the electrons, and add dephasing. Further attenuation on the colder stages is needed.

3. Why is a directional coupler placed at the mixing chamber instead of at room temperature?

Show answer
If the incoming and reflected waves were separated at room temperature, the reflected signal would have to travel back up through all the attenuators on the input line, losing tens of decibels before reaching any amplifier. With a cold coupler, the reflected signal goes straight into a low-loss output line and the 4 K amplifier, preserving its signal-to-noise ratio.

Back matter

Glossary

Every term defined in the text, in alphabetical order. Click a term to jump to where it is first explained.

bias tee
A circuit that adds a slowly varying (DC) voltage, delivered through a resistor or inductor, to a fast signal delivered through a capacitor, so both reach the same gate. (Chapter 3 · From chip to sample holder)
electric-dipole spin resonance
Electric-dipole spin resonance: driving spin rotations with an oscillating electric field, which shakes the electron in a magnetic-field gradient (micromagnet) or acts through spin-orbit coupling. (Chapter 2 · The device we will follow)
electron temperature
The temperature that describes the energy distribution (Fermi function) of electrons in the device's reservoirs; usually higher than the fridge temperature because of noise and weak electron–phonon coupling. (Chapter 4 · The fridge as part of the experiment)
lever arm
The ratio between a change in a gate voltage and the resulting change in a dot's electrochemical potential, usually quoted in eV/V or µeV/mV. (Chapter 1 · The whole experiment on one page)
ohmic contacts
A low-resistance electrical contact to the 2D electron gas, made in Si by implanting phosphorus to form a degenerately doped n++ region, and in GaAs by annealing a Ni/Ge/Au alloy. (Chapter 2 · The device we will follow)
overlapping-gate architecture
A gate design in which several metal layers, separated by thin oxide, overlap so that each gate controls one feature (a dot or a barrier) with little cross-talk; introduced for Si by Angus, Zajac and Borselli and co-workers. (Chapter 2 · The device we will follow)
randomized benchmarking
A protocol that applies long random sequences of gates and measures how fast the survival probability decays, giving an average error per gate that is insensitive to preparation and measurement errors. (Chapter 1 · The whole experiment on one page)
undoped
A heterostructure with no intentional dopants; the 2D electron gas exists only where positive gate voltages accumulate it, drawing electrons from implanted ohmic contacts. (Chapter 2 · The device we will follow)
valley splitting
The energy separating the two lowest valley states of an electron in a Si quantum dot, set by the atomic-scale structure of the interface; typically tens to a few hundred µeV in Si/SiGe. (Chapter 2 · The device we will follow)
valleys
Equivalent minima of the conduction band in k-space. Bulk Si has six; tensile strain in a Si/SiGe well lowers the two along the growth direction, and the interface splits those two by the valley splitting. (Chapter 2 · The device we will follow)
visibility
The contrast of a measured oscillation, equal to 1 − α − β for readout error probabilities α and β; also F↑ + F↓ − 1. (Chapter 1 · The whole experiment on one page)
